orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the May 17, 2011 order granting defense summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants' motion for summary judgment and dismissed the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped at the duct-taped junction of a permanent and seasonal rug inside defendants' store entrance. Accounts differed about the height differential and tape condition; plaintiff's friend described the tape as still secured after the accident.

legal_issues.finding: Considering the photograph, dimensions and accident circumstances, the court found the defect too trivial to be actionable and no triable issue that it constituted a trap, snare or nuisance.
The court recounted the defense engineer's height measurement as part of the dimensional record supporting its triviality determination; it did not announce a separate expert-admissibility ruling.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff described a raised/wrinkled taped junction but had not observed it before falling and could not recall whether it was pulled up afterward.
Plaintiff's friend estimated a half-inch differential and described the tape as still secured after the fall.
Defendants' engineer measured a five-sixteenths to three-eighths inch differential.
The court examined a photograph of the alleged carpeting defect when assessing triviality.

quality.notes: Store-interior control is supported without assuming legal title. Customer role is supported by the source's reference to no other customers nearby. Distinct estimates of height and tape condition are preserved. Unobstructed view supports the contextual triviality analysis, not a separate finding under the open-and-obvious doctrine. No negligence/notice finding is inferred from the physical rug arrangement. Preserve source OCR in the photograph quotation and page marker. Accident date is unstated.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.
Memorandum: Plaintiff commenced this action seeking damages for injuries she sustained when she allegedly tripped and fell on carpeting at defendants’ store.

Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Onondaga County (James P. Murphy, J.), entered May 17, 2011 in a personal injury action. The order granted the motion of defendants for summary judgment and dismissed the complaint.

The allegedly defective condition was created by two rugs inside an entrance to defendants’ store. The first rug was permanent, inset into the floor and flush with the tile surrounding it. The second rug was seasonal, approximately one-quarter-inch thick, and it was placed on top of the tile floor and adjacent to the permanent rug during inclement weather. The permanent and seasonal rugs were duct taped together at the edge where they met.
Plaintiff testified at her deposition that she tripped and fell on a portion of the duct tape covering the “raised” area or “hump” created by the adjoining rugs.

Although plaintiff did not testify with respect to the extent of the height differential between the rugs, plaintiff’s friend, who was with plaintiff at the time of the accident and who felt the raised area under the duct tape immediately thereafter, estimated at her deposition that the height differential was one-half of an inch.
Defendants’ expert engineer measured that the height differential between *1475 the rugs was between five-sixteenths and three-eighths of an inch.

Although plaintiff testified that it felt as though her foot got caught in the duct tape, which, according to plaintiff, was “raised a little” and “wrinkled,” plaintiff did not observe the tape before she fell, and she could not recall whether the tape was “pulled up” from the rugs thereafter.
Plaintiff’s friend testified that, after the accident, the tape was “still secured to the carpet,” was not “raised up or bubbled up” and was not “lifted up or pulled up in any way.”
The accident occurred on a sunny day, and plaintiff testified that there were no other customers in the vicinity and that nothing blocked her view of the area in which she was walking.

“After examining the photograph! ] depicting the width, depth and irregularity of the defect in the [carpeting], and in view of the time, place and circumstances of plaintiff’s injury, we conclude that defendants established as a matter of law that the defect is too trivial to be actionable”
We further conclude that plaintiff “failed to raise a triable issue of fact whether the alleged defect has the characteristics of a trap, snare or nuisance”

orders.description: Defendant's appeal from the April 14, 2021 order denying summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff fell while descending an interior staircase in defendant's building on December 21, 2017. A handrail was present on the right but absent on the left; the initiating mechanism was not identified.

legal_issues.finding: Plaintiff raised no triable issue that failure to install a second handrail breached the reasonably-safe-staircase common-law duty.
Defendant established that plaintiff did not know what caused the fall; the second-handrail theories did not raise a triable issue under the applicable code or common-law duty.
Defendant established the building was not subject to plaintiff's cited provisions; plaintiff raised no triable issue that a second handrail was legally required.

quality.notes: Private ownership is explicit, but the actual-case account establishes only a stairway fall, not a slip/trip. This is mechanism review, not exclusion merely because plaintiff failed to prove negligent causation. The quoted general rule about a misstep/reaching for a handrail does not establish those acts in this case. Building use, plaintiff's role and specific evidence formats are unstated; no deposition or expert evidence is inferred. Apply unchanged rules to this preliminary validation-period case.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.
On December 21, 2017, at approximately 12:45 p.m., the plaintiff fell down a staircase inside a building owned by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (R. Bruce Cozzens, Jr., J.), entered April 14, 2021. The order denied the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
As the plaintiff descended the stairs, there was a handrail on the right side but not on the left side of the staircase.
Here, the defendant established, prima facie, that the plaintiff did not know what had caused her to fall
The defendant also established, prima facie, that the building was not subject to the particular code provisions relied upon by the plaintiff
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to whether there was an applicable statutory or code provision that required a second handrail on the staircase.

The plaintiff also failed to raise a triable issue of fact as to whether the defendant breached her common-law duty to maintain the staircase in a reasonably safe condition by failing to install a second handrail
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the order entered on or about April 1, 2009 granting summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff slipped on wet linoleum in defendants' supermarket vestibule during all-day rain and observed no mats or warning signs. A grocery clerk described a general mat practice but did not recall conditions or mats on the accident date.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants' ongoing-rain argument did not justify dismissal; the testimony supported a triable failure to take reasonable remedial measures.
Plaintiff's account raised a knew-or-should-have-known factual question; the employee's lack of recollection did not establish defendants' lack of actual knowledge.
Testimony about the wet floor and mat practice supported a triable visible/apparent condition of sufficient duration. Independently, defendants failed their initial lack-of-notice showing.

The court disagreed with the lower court's recurrent-rain-condition reasoning, considering plaintiff's account and the store's inclement-weather mat practice sufficient for a factual issue; it did not conclusively establish a known recurring defect.
Plaintiff identified the wet slippery floor as the cause; his firsthand account was not mere speculation.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiff's firsthand wet-floor and missing-mat/sign account supported causation and notice issues.
Grocery clerk described general mat practices but lacked recollection of the accident day's weather and measures; this did not establish lack of notice.

quality.notes: Private supermarket-interior control supported without inferring title. Plaintiff's role and accident date are unstated. Preserve both the sufficiency of opposition and the independent failure of defendants' initial burden; neither is a final liability verdict. General practices do not establish mats actually present that day. Rain is supplied through testimony, not identified weather records. No distinct snow/ice storm-in-progress holding is inferred from the ongoing-rain duty argument.

evidence.quote: Order, Supreme Court, New York County (Debra A. James, J.), entered on or about April 1, 2009, which, in an action for personal injuries sustained in a slip and fall on a wet floor in the vestibule of defendants’ supermarket, granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, unanimously reversed, on the law, without costs, the motion denied, and the complaint reinstated.

As plaintiff entered defendants’ supermarket, he slipped and fell in the vestibule, which was covered in linoleum tiles that were wet because “[i]t was raining all day and coming in.” He observed no mats or signs warning of a slippery condition.

At his examination before trial, defendants’ grocery clerk testified that, when it rained, “somebody would go and get some mats and put them in the front,” but he did not remember whether he had ever seen “the porter place down mats in the vestibule area when it was raining.”
Nor did he recall what the weather was like on the day of the accident or whether he had seen “any mats down in the vestibule area that day.”

On their motion, defendants denied actual or constructive knowledge of the alleged hazardous condition, contending that they had no duty to provide an ongoing remedy when a slippery condition is caused by moisture tracked into the premises during a constant rain.

Supreme Court agreed, reasoning that plaintiff “failed to submit evidence sufficient to raise an issue of fact as to constructive notice that there was a recurrent dangerous condition with respect to rainy weather conditions.” We disagree.

Plaintiff s statement that the floor was wet and slippery due to a constant rain is evidence sufficient to raise a factual question as to whether defendant knew or should have known of the *440 existence of a hazardous condition.
Plaintiff identified the wet and slippery floor as the reason for his fall; thus, his testimony cannot be dismissed as mere speculation regarding causation
In addition, defendants’ employee testified that it was the store’s practice to put down mats during inclement weather.

Together, the testimony satisfies plaintiffs burden to demonstrate that a visible and apparent hazardous condition had existed for a sufficient length of time to permit defendants’ employees to discover and remedy it
but that they failed to take reasonable measures to do so.

In any event, defendants’ moving papers failed to make out a prima facie case for summary judgment. The testimony of defendants’ employee does not establish that defendants lacked actual or constructive knowledge of the condition of their vestibule, only that the employee had no recollection of conditions or remedial measures that might have been implemented on the date of the accident

orders.description: Defendant's appeal from the April 29, 2014 order denying summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing plaintiff's complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on steps at defendant's residential property. The record concerned snow on the steps and an alternative theory involving rotten, deteriorated stair boards.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant failed to establish an ongoing storm: plaintiff's equivocal testimony did not distinguish current-storm snow from prior accumulations.
A factual issue remained whether deteriorated stair boards caused or contributed to the injuries, even assuming a storm defense; defendant had not addressed that theory.
The opposition did not create a feigned issue by contradicting prior testimony: plaintiff had not been questioned about the unsafe stairs at deposition.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant submitted plaintiff's equivocal snow deposition; his later stair-condition submissions were not inconsistent with an unasked deposition subject.

quality.notes: Private residential ownership and slip are explicit. Do not infer tenancy or family relationship from the shared surname. No accident date is stated. Snow-source and deteriorated-board theories remain unresolved; no actual/constructive-notice determination or weather-record evidence is inferred. Opposing submissions are not identified as an affidavit and are not relabeled as one.

evidence.quote: It is hereby ordered that the order so appealed from is unanimously affirmed without costs.
Memorandum: Plaintiff commenced this action seeking damages for injuries he allegedly sustained when he slipped and fell on the steps of residential property owned by defendant.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Onondaga County (Anthony J. Paris, J.), entered April 29, 2014. The order denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing plaintiff’s complaint.
We conclude that defendant failed to establish as a matter of law that there was a storm in progress at the time of plaintiff’s accident

Plaintiff’s equivocal deposition testimony, which defendant submitted in support of her motion, was insufficient to establish that the snow on the steps “was the result of an ongoing storm as opposed to an accumulation of [snow] from . . . prior snowfalls”

In addition, the court properly determined that, even assuming, arguendo, defendant was entitled to judgment based upon the storm in progress doctrine, there is an issue of fact whether the rotten and deteriorated condition of the boards on the staircase caused or contributed to plaintiff’s injuries.
Indeed, we note that defendant did not address that theory of liability in her motion

In any event, we reject defendant’s contention that plaintiff’s opposing submissions in support of that theory of liability were “merely an attempt to raise a feigned issue of fact” to defeat the motion
Plaintiff was not questioned at his deposition with respect to the allegedly unsafe condition of the stairs and, thus, his submissions did not contradict his deposition testimony on that issue.
Supreme Court properly denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiff's appeal from the October 11, 2012 order granting summary judgment.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly tripped in an aisle of defendants' store. After falling, he saw three folded beach chairs stacked and leaning against the aisle wall.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants established both obviousness and lack of inherent danger; plaintiff raised no triable issue.
Defendants argued plaintiff did not know the cause. The appellate court resolved the case on obviousness/non-dangerousness and did not separately decide this ground.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendants submitted plaintiff's deposition describing chairs seen after his fall.

quality.notes: Private store-interior control supported without assuming title. A personal trip is explicit despite the disputed negligent cause. Chairs observed afterward are not treated as a conclusively established cause. Both obviousness and lack of inherent danger support dismissal; no separate causation or notice holding is invented. Plaintiff's role and accident date are unstated.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly tripped and fell in one of the aisles of the defendants’ store and sustained injuries.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Marber, J.), entered October 11, 2012, which granted the defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

The defendants moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, contending that the plaintiff did not know what had caused him to fall and that, in any event, the alleged hazardous condition was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous.

In support of the motion, the defendants submitted, inter alia, the deposition testimony of the plaintiff wherein he stated that after he fell, he saw three folded-up beach chairs stacked and leaning against the wall in the aisle.
The defendants established their entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating, prima facie, that the condition at issue was open and obvious and not inherently dangerous
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
Based upon the foregoing determination, the plaintiff’s remaining contention has been rendered academic.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
